notes: Ruling slot 4 = PCR under Ceauşescu (MD sprite ROM_communist_state, same-named party). Following MD, King Michael's Royal House sits in slot 0 and the rival Lambrino line in slot 23 (both ROM_monarchist), and the Hungarian minority body sits in slot 16 where MD places the UDMR. PNŢ (1) and PNL (2) keep their MD sprites. Dej's old guard as neo-Stalinist slot 6, Securitate (CSS) in 7, Maurer's technocrats in 13, Pătrăşcanu's rehabilitated reform-communist legacy in 19, UTC under Iliescu in 5. The Petroleum and Gas Institute is still in Bucharest in 1970 (moved to Ploieşti only in 1975).

0.name: Casa Regală a României
0.text:
The Royal House of Romania is headed by King Michael I, who reigned from 1940 until the Communists forced his abdication on 30 December 1947. Michael, who led the coup of 23 August 1944 that took Romania out of the Axis war, lives in Versoix near Geneva with Queen Anne and their five daughters, earning his living in business and kept at arm's length by Bucharest.

The King stands for the constitution of 1923, parliamentary democracy, the Western orientation of the old kingdom and the Orthodox and national values of the dynasty. Western governments receive him with respect, and Radio Free Europe ensures that his name is not forgotten at home. His leverage lies in legitimacy: for millions of older Romanians he remains the lawful sovereign.

1.name: Partidul Naţional Ţărănesc
1.text:
The National Peasants' Party, formed in 1926 from Iuliu Maniu's Transylvanian National Party and the Peasants' Party of the Old Kingdom, was the great democratic force of interwar Romania. Outlawed in 1947 after a staged trial, it lost Maniu and Ion Mihalache in communist prisons. At home its heir is Maniu's former secretary Corneliu Coposu, who emerged in 1964 from seventeen years of prison and forced residence; abroad it is represented by Ion Raţiu in London and by Constantin Vişoianu's Romanian National Committee in Washington.

It stands for parliamentary democracy, private peasant property, Christian values and alliance with the West. Close to the outlawed Greek-Catholic Church of Transylvania, it keeps a silent following among older peasants and the provincial intelligentsia, which is its main leverage.

2.name: Partidul Naţional Liberal
2.text:
The National Liberal Party, founded in 1875 and long led by the Brătianu dynasty, built modern Romania's institutions, its banks and the constitution of 1923. Dissolved in 1947, it lost its leader Dinu Brătianu and the historian Gheorghe Brătianu in the prison of Sighet. In 1970 it survives as memory and as a network of survivors, among them Radu Câmpeanu, a liberal youth leader of the 1940s who spent years in communist prisons.

Its tradition is constitutional monarchy, private enterprise, a strong national bourgeoisie, Western investment on Romanian terms and the rule of law. Its old base of merchants, lawyers and bankers has been destroyed, but the Brătianu name still carries weight. Its leverage lies in history and in its contacts with the emigration in Paris and New York.

3.name: Partidul Social Democrat Român
3.text:
The Romanian Social Democratic Party, rooted in the workers' movement of the 1890s, split in 1946 when Constantin Titel Petrescu refused to run on a common list with the Communists. His Independent Social Democratic Party was crushed and Titel Petrescu died in 1957 after years in prison, while the fusionist wing merged into the Romanian Workers' Party in 1948. Some of its men, such as Ştefan Voitec, President of the Grand National Assembly, serve the regime; the independent tradition lives on in exile.

The party stands for parliamentary democracy, free trade unions, a mixed economy and the solidarity of the Socialist International. Its old cadres among railwaymen, printers and skilled workers have dwindled, and its leverage lies in exile contacts with Western labour parties.

4.name: Partidul Comunist Român
4.text:
The Romanian Communist Party, founded in 1921 and renamed from the Romanian Workers' Party in 1965, holds a monopoly of power. Nicolae Ceauşescu, who succeeded Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej in March 1965, is General Secretary and, since December 1967, President of the State Council; the Tenth Congress of August 1969 confirmed his supremacy, with Ion Gheorghe Maurer as Prime Minister. His refusal to join the invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968 made him a national hero.

The party pursues national communism: forced industrialisation, independence from Moscow within the Warsaw Pact and ties with China, Israel, West Germany and the United States, whose President Nixon visited Bucharest in August 1969. At home it combines patriotism with strict control and a ban on abortion. Its leverage is total, from the nomenklatura to the Securitate.

5.name: Uniunea Tineretului Comunist
5.text:
The Union of Communist Youth is the party's mass organisation for young people in factories, villages and schools, with millions of members. Since 1967 it has been led by First Secretary Ion Iliescu, a Moscow-trained engineer who doubles as Minister for Youth Affairs, and in August 1968 it channelled the wave of patriotic enthusiasm that followed Ceauşescu's defiance of the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia.

Its activists see themselves as the vanguard of a modern, industrial and independent Romania, impatient with old bureaucrats and eager for technical education, great construction sites and youth brigades. Iliescu's circle favours a more open, technocratic socialism. Its leverage lies in its numbers, its control over young people's careers and its role as the nursery of the next generation of party cadres.

6.name: Baronii lui Dej
6.text:
Dej's Barons are the old guard of Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej, the Stalinist leader who ruled Romania until his death in 1965. Ceauşescu has been dismantling them one by one: in April 1968 he rehabilitated the executed communist Lucreţiu Pătrăşcanu and expelled Alexandru Drăghici, Dej's feared security chief, from the leadership; Chivu Stoica lost the presidency of the State Council in 1967, and Gheorghe Apostol has been pushed to the margins.

They resent the cult growing around Ceauşescu, his courting of Western leaders and his risky defiance of Moscow, and they long for the collective discipline and orthodoxy of the 1950s. Many still have friends in the Soviet embassy and in the security services they once commanded. Their leverage is waning: old networks, compromising files and hopes of Soviet support.

7.name: Consiliul Securităţii Statului
7.text:
The Securitate, Romania's political police since 1948, was reorganised in April 1968 as the State Security Council, a body separate from the Interior Ministry and chaired by Ion Stănescu. Ceauşescu used the reform to purge the officers of the Drăghici era and to bind the service to himself, while its counter-intelligence turned its attention to Soviet agents inside Romania.

As a power bloc the Securitate stands for order, secrecy and national sovereignty under one leader. It watches émigrés, churches, minorities, writers and students, runs tens of thousands of informers and quietly sells exit visas to Jews and Germans for hard currency. Its leverage lies in its files, its control of borders and passports, and its value to a regime that trusts no one.

8.name: Halqat al-Sadr
8.text:
The Sadr Circle is a small group of Iraqi Shia students at the Petroleum and Gas Institute and the Polytechnic in Bucharest, part of the steady flow of Arab engineers trained in Romania. Its members read Ayatollah Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr of Najaf, whose books Falsafatuna and Iqtisaduna answer Marxism with an Islamic philosophy and economics, and some have ties to the clandestine Islamic Da'wa Party.

They want an Islamic state that is modern, just and constitutional, guided by the sharia yet open to science and planning, as an alternative to both Ba'athist dictatorship and communism. Watched by the Securitate and the Iraqi embassy alike, they have no local leverage, but they will return home as engineers of the oil industry and of the Islamic movement.

9.name: Anjoman-e Eslami
9.text:
The Islamic Society is a handful of Iranian students in Bucharest, sent under the cultural agreements between the Shah's government and Ceauşescu's Romania, who have turned to the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini. Banished in 1964 after denouncing the Shah's White Revolution and the immunity granted to American military personnel, Khomeini teaches in Najaf, and his letters and recorded sermons circulate among Iranian students abroad.

They condemn the Shah as a puppet of America and Israel, reject both Western liberalism and Marxism, and believe that the learned clergy should guide the nation. Their position is delicate, for Bucharest courts the Shah for oil and trade. Their leverage in Romania is nil, but they belong to a growing network of Islamic student associations across Europe.

10.name: Muftiatul Cultului Musulman din România
10.english: Muftiate of the Muslim Community of Romania
10.text:
The Muftiate of the Muslim Community of Romania, seated in Constanţa beside the Carol I Mosque, is the officially recognised body of some 40,000 Muslims, the Turks and Tatars of Dobruja whose ancestors settled there under Ottoman rule. Its mufti and imams are paid and supervised by the Department of Religious Affairs, and the community keeps historic mosques such as the Esmahan Sultan Mosque of Mangalia.

The Muftiate is loyal to the state and to the Hanafi tradition: it asks for permission to train imams, repair mosques, print the Koran and send a few pilgrims to Mecca, while presenting Romania to Arab and Turkish visitors as a tolerant country. Its leverage is modest but real, for Ceauşescu values the goodwill of the Arab and Muslim world.

11.name: Halqat al-Nabhani
11.text:
The Nabhani Circle is a cell of Jordanian and Palestinian medical students in Iaşi and Bucharest who belong to Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Islamic Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the judge Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani. Banned and hunted by the Arab regimes, the party survives in secret cells, and its students abroad meet in hostel rooms to study its books.

They reject nationalism, socialism and parliamentary democracy as foreign creeds and hold that only a restored caliphate ruling by the sharia can unite the Muslims and liberate Palestine. Disdainful of the guerrilla groups now dominating Palestinian politics, they seek to win over army officers for a single seizure of power. Their leverage in Romania is nil, but their ideas travel home with every graduate.

12.name: Mecidiye Medresesi Mezunları
12.text:
The Graduates of the Medgidia Seminary are the imams, teachers and pious notables of Dobruja's Turkish and Tatar villages who were trained at the Muslim seminary of Medgidia, the community's only school of religious learning until the authorities closed it in the 1960s. Without it the Muftiate struggles to replace ageing imams, and religious knowledge passes privately from fathers to sons.

They want the seminary reopened, Turkish and Tatar teaching restored, the Koran taught to children and mosque associations allowed to manage their own property. Like the Muslim Brotherhood they believe in revival through education, piety and community work rather than confrontation, and they respect the state. Their leverage lies in the trust of the villages, links with Turkey and the cohesion of a small community.

13.name: Tehnocraţii lui Maurer
13.text:
Maurer's Technocrats are the managers of state and economy who gather around Ion Gheorghe Maurer, Prime Minister since 1961, an urbane lawyer and, with Gheorghiu-Dej, the architect of the April 1964 declaration of independence within the communist movement. Around him work the planners of the State Planning Committee, the foreign trade ministry and the economists who negotiate credits and licences with Western firms.

They want Romania to industrialise with Western technology, as with the Renault licence behind the Dacia car, to diversify trade away from Comecon and to join Western economic institutions, while avoiding ideological adventures. Loyal to Ceauşescu, they are uneasy at his growing personal power. Their leverage lies in expertise, foreign contacts and the regime's need for growth.

14.name: Biserica Ortodoxă Română
14.text:
The Romanian Orthodox Church, a patriarchate since 1925, embraces the great majority of Romanians. Patriarch Justinian Marina, enthroned in 1948 with communist support, has preserved its parishes, seminaries and monasteries through a policy of 'social apostolate', accepting state supervision and praising the regime while quietly protecting clergy, even as thousands of priests and monks passed through the prisons of the 1950s.

The Church stands for Orthodox faith, national tradition and the unity of the Romanian people, and it gains from Ceauşescu's patriotic course. It absorbed the outlawed Greek-Catholic Church in 1948 and treats the matter as closed. Neither pro-Western nor pro-Soviet, it is the nation's oldest institution, and its leverage lies in rural faith, the monasteries and the loyalty of the villages.

15.name: Directorii de combinat
15.text:
The Combine Directors are the managers of Romania's giant industrial projects: the new iron and steel combine at Galaţi on the Danube, the Dacia car works at Piteşti, the refineries and petrochemical plants of Ploieşti, the tractor and truck works of Braşov and the old engineering works of Reşiţa. Promoted by Ceauşescu's drive to industrialise at any cost, they command vast budgets and armies of workers drawn from the villages.

They want ever larger investment, Western machinery and priority over agriculture and consumer goods, while accepting no market test of their efficiency. Tied to county party chiefs and ministries, they are the regime's most powerful economic lobby. Their leverage lies in the share of national income they absorb and in Ceauşescu's personal pride in every new plant.

16.name: Magyar Nemzetiségű Dolgozók Tanácsa
16.english: Council of Working People of Hungarian Nationality
16.text:
The Council of Working People of Hungarian Nationality was created in November 1968, together with a German counterpart, when Ceauşescu sought the loyalty of the minorities after the invasion of Czechoslovakia. It is the only body that speaks for Romania's 1.6 million Hungarians, and its best-known figures are János Fazekas, a member of the party leadership, and Károly Király, party chief of the Hungarian-majority Covasna county.

Its members want Hungarian schools, a revival of the Hungarian university in Cluj that was merged away in 1959, cultural freedom and local self-government for the Székely Land. Many also look to Bishop Áron Márton of Alba Iulia, freed from house arrest in 1967. Its leverage lies in numbers, in Budapest's attention and in the regime's need for calm in Transylvania.

17.name: Comisia pentru Ocrotirea Monumentelor Naturii
17.english: Commission for the Protection of Natural Monuments
17.text:
The Commission for the Protection of Natural Monuments, attached to the Romanian Academy, was founded in 1930 under the impulse of the botanist Alexandru Borza and the biologist Emil Racoviţă, and it created the Retezat National Park in 1935. Borza, now in his eighties in Cluj, remains its patriarch, while a network of botanists, zoologists and foresters supervises reserves from the Danube Delta to the Carpathian peaks.

It defends rare species and landscapes against the pressures of crash industrialisation: reed harvesting and drainage in the Delta, logging in the mountains, hydroelectric dams and the smoke of new chemical plants. It speaks in the language of science and patriotism, presenting nature as national heritage. Its leverage lies in the prestige of the Academy and in sympathetic local officials.

18.name: Frontul Unităţii Socialiste
18.text:
The Socialist Unity Front was founded in November 1968 to replace the old People's Democratic Front, uniting under the party's leadership the trade unions, the youth and women's organisations, the cooperatives, the councils of the Hungarian and German minorities and other mass bodies. Ceauşescu chairs its National Council, and its non-party faces include veterans of Petru Groza's Ploughmen's Front and social democrats who joined the regime.

It presents socialism as the cause of the whole nation, beyond class and ethnicity, and gives Romania's independent foreign course a mass base. Its programme is broad: social welfare, cooperative agriculture, national unity and friendship with all peoples, East, West and Third World alike. Its leverage lies in its reach into every workplace and village and its role as the regime's electoral machine.

19.name: Moştenitorii lui Pătrăşcanu
19.text:
Pătrăşcanu's Heirs are the communist intellectuals who see in Lucreţiu Pătrăşcanu, the party's leading theorist, minister of justice after 1944 and victim of a show trial ending in his execution in 1954, the model of a Romanian, humane and lawful socialism. His rehabilitation in April 1968 gave them a hero, and survivors of his trial such as the economist Belu Zilber and the folklorist Harry Brauner have returned to public life.

They want socialism without terror: the rule of law, freedom of research and creation, an honest reckoning with the crimes of the 1950s and national independence pursued by reason rather than a leader's cult. They watch Ceauşescu's growing power with unease. Their leverage lies in universities, institutes and literary journals, and in a martyr the regime itself has honoured.

20.name: România Mare
20.text:
Greater Romania is the nationalist current that has flourished since Ceauşescu made patriotism the regime's creed, after the party in 1964 allowed the publication of Karl Marx's notes condemning Russia's annexation of Bessarabia. Its voices are writers such as the novelist Eugen Barbu and the young poet Adrian Păunescu, together with historians who celebrate the Dacians, the medieval voivodes and the union of 1918.

It dreams of recovering Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina from the Soviet Union, distrusts the Hungarian minority and any talk of Transylvanian autonomy, and exalts the Romanian peasant, the army and the national leader. Anti-Russian and suspicious of Western cosmopolitanism, it wants a strong, ethnically confident state. Its leverage lies in the press, the Writers' Union and a leadership that finds nationalism useful.

21.name: Mişcarea Legionară
21.text:
The Legionary Movement, the Iron Guard founded by Corneliu Zelea Codreanu in 1927, ruled Romania with Marshal Ion Antonescu in 1940-1941 until its failed rebellion and pogrom of January 1941 drove its leaders into German exile. Since 1945 its commander Horia Sima has led the movement from Madrid under Franco's protection, while thousands of legionaries passed through communist prisons and the 're-education' of Piteşti.

It preaches an Orthodox mystical nationalism: a spiritual 'new man', the cult of martyrs, antisemitism, anti-communism and a Romania purified of foreign influence. In exile it publishes papers and keeps chapters in Spain, West Germany and the Americas, though split by quarrels over Sima's leadership. Its leverage is small, but the Securitate takes it seriously and infiltrates it relentlessly.

22.name: Forţele Armate ale Republicii Socialiste România
22.native_full: Forţele Armate ale Republicii Socialiste România
22.text:
The Romanian Armed Forces, about 170,000 strong, are commanded by Defence Minister General Ion Ioniţă and Chief of the General Staff General Ion Gheorghe. Romania has hosted no Soviet garrison since 1958, and after the invasion of Czechoslovakia Ceauşescu created the Patriotic Guards, a mass militia of workers and peasants, and began building a doctrine of 'war of the entire people'.

The officer corps is trained to defend national territory against any aggressor, a thinly veiled reference to the Soviet Union, and resists Warsaw Pact command integration and manoeuvres on Romanian soil. It wants modern equipment from every source and a domestic arms industry. Its leverage lies in the regime's need for a credible deterrent, though party commissars and Securitate counter-intelligence keep it tightly controlled.

23.name: Ramura Lambrino
23.native_full: Ramura Lambrino a Casei de Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen
23.text:
The Lambrino branch descends from the first, annulled marriage of the future King Carol II to Zizi Lambrino in 1918. Their son Carol Mircea Grigore, born in 1920 and living in France, has fought for years in the courts to be recognised as Carol II's legitimate eldest son and thus as rightful head of the royal house in place of his half-brother, King Michael. His son Paul, born in 1948, shares the claim.

The branch presents itself as a Romanian, Orthodox and popular alternative to Michael's line, untouched by the abdication of 1947. It has no organisation inside Romania and little support in the emigration, where most monarchists remain loyal to Michael. Its leverage lies in legal arguments and the readiness of some émigrés to look for another king.
